newsitem.title: USA: EchoStar, News Corp deal hits snag.
newsitem.headline: EchoStar, News Corp deal hits snag.

text.p: The deal between EchoStar Communications Corp and News Corp Ltd to build a direct-TV satellite hit a snag Monday, seemingly over an issue analysts said was the least of the venture's worries.
EchoStar issued a statement early Monday saying News Corp's planned $1 billion investment was delayed over News Corp's request to abandon its existing conditional-access system.

While analysts viewed the deal as salvageable, some said there appear to be other issues at play -- not the least of which are two strong-willed businessmen who are not accustomed to the give-and-take of 50-50 partnerships and may be battling for greater control.

Still other analysts said News Corp Chairman and Chief Executive Rupert Murdoch may have had second thoughts about investing more than $1 billion in a venture that faces regulatory hurdles, as well as intense competition inside and outside the industry.

"It seems kind of odd it would be a reason," NatWest Securities analyst Gary Farber said. "It's kind of like if you're going to get married to somebody and you couldn't agree on the band so you call off the wedding."

Ted Henderson, managing director of research at Janco Partners said: "It's the one concrete issue they're willing to hang their hat on. But they're probably more meat on the bones of the other issues."
EchoStar's stock closed down 2-3/8 at 14-3/8. News Corp's stock remained unchanged on the New York Stock exchange, hovering at about 18-3/8.
The alliance faces several regulatory issues, including Hart-Scott-Rodino, foreign ownership questions and U.S. copyright laws.
Some analysts said the two companies may have differences in opinion over how to proceed in dealing with those regulatory matters.
Nevertheless, most analysts expressed skepticism about the conditional-access reason given by EchoStar in News Corp's delay in its planned $1 billion investment, saying it seemed a small matter.

Conditional access is an encryption service that allows subscribers to view only those channels for which they have paid. EchoStar currently uses the Nagra SA system, while News Corp has a stake in another vendor.
"This does not seem to me to be a deal-breaker issue," Smith Barney analyst John Reidy said.

Instead, some analysts said there likely are other matters at hand, including the strong personalities of Murdoch and EchoStar President, Chairman and Chief Executive Charles Ergen, each of whom is used to being in charge.

In addition, some analysts speculated that Murdoch may have grown wary of investing more than $1 billion on a venture in which News Corp would be a late player and may be seeking improved terms from EchoStar.

"I think there are two very strong personalities with Charles and Rupert," said Bob Scherman, editor and publisher of Satellite Business News magazine. "They are both playing chicken right now. I don't know who's going to blink first."
Henderson said: "Murdoch and Ergen, from the day this deal came out, people were saying, 'Boy, it's hard to those guys working together.'"

There have been recent reports that Murdoch had approached Tele-Communications Inc Chief Executive John Malone about a possible alliance with Primestar, a satellite partnership made up of six companies.

News Corp spokesman Jim Platt would not comment on those reports, or on EchoStar's statement except to say: "The only comment is we won't be making any (regulatory) filings until we resolve some issues with them."
Primestar spokeswoman Katie Stephan said she was not aware of any recent conversations with News Corp.
"Nothing came of that," she said. "I'm not aware we've been approached again."

When it was announced in February, the two companies said their direct-broadcast venture would offer as many as 500 channels of digital TV, Internet services and local broadcast TV signals to markets across the United States.
It was viewed as competition to DirecTV, which is owned by General Motors Corp Hughes Electronics and AT&T Corp and Primestar, which is owned by a host of cable TV operators.
Those two providers have the largest block of the direct-broadcast satellite industry's 4.5 million subscribers, with EchoStar distantly behind.

The News Corp-EchoStar venture was to begin delivering programs to U.S. households early next year under the News Corp American Sky Broadcasting name. It remains to be seen if the venture will actually be launched. Even as it was announced in February, some analysts viewed it as a late entry by Murdoch to get into the market in 1998. The intense competition in the field may be an incentive to remain in a partnership, analysts said.

"Both companies are at a disadvantage without each other," Lazard Freres analyst John Hodulik said. "Going it alone, they are 2-3 years behind their main competitor...It's not dead. the deal still certainly makes sense."
